concepts.name: Series connection
concepts.statement: Resistors are in series whenever the flow of charge must pass through them one after the other, so that there is only one path and every resistor carries the same current. The book's own example is a person holding a screwdriver: the shaft, the handle, the body and the shoes are four resistances the same current must cross in turn. Recognizing the connection is what decides which of the two combination rules applies, so it comes before either of them.

concepts.name: Resistance in series
concepts.statement: Since all of the current must pass through each resistor, it meets the resistance of each in turn, and the resistances simply add. The result follows from conservation of energy: the energy the source gives a charge is the energy the resistors take from it, so the source's voltage is the sum of the voltage drops, and dividing by the common current leaves the sum of the resistances. It is the rule that says a longer cord or a thicker sole reduces the current.

concepts.name: Voltage division in series
concepts.statement: The energy supplied to a charge by the source is the energy the resistors take from it, since there is nowhere else for the energy to go. Writing that energy as $qV$ on both sides and canceling the charge leaves the voltage of the source as the sum of the voltage drops across the resistors. Individual resistors in series do not each get the source's whole voltage; they divide it in proportion to their resistances.

concepts.name: Parallel connection
concepts.statement: Resistors are in parallel when each one is connected directly to the voltage source by wires of negligible resistance, so that each has the full voltage of the source across it and draws the current it would draw if it were alone. That is why a house, a car and every power distribution system is wired in parallel: each device gets the same voltage and works independently of the others.

concepts.name: Resistance in parallel
concepts.statement: Each branch has the source's full voltage, so the current in each is that voltage divided by its own resistance, and conservation of charge makes the source's current the sum of the branch currents. Factoring the voltage out of the sum leaves the reciprocals of the resistances adding, which is the rule for a parallel connection. Adding a branch adds a path, so it always raises the current and lowers the total resistance.

concepts.name: Current division in parallel
concepts.statement: Charge is conserved, so whatever current the source drives out must be exactly the current the branches carry between them. Parallel resistors do not each get the total current; they divide it, and the smallest resistance takes the largest share. This is the statement conservation of charge makes about a parallel connection, as the sum of the voltages is the statement conservation of energy makes about a series one.

concepts.name: Least resistance of a parallel combination
concepts.statement: When resistors are connected in parallel, more current flows from the source than would flow through any one of them alone, so the total resistance must be lower than the lowest of them. The reciprocals add, and a sum of reciprocals is larger than any one of them, so its inverse is smaller than the smallest resistance. It is the result that decides whether a circuit has been reduced correctly, since a parallel total larger than one of its parts is an arithmetic mistake.

concepts.name: Reducing a resistor network
concepts.statement: More complex connections of resistors are often just combinations of series and parallel parts, and wire resistance in series with parallel devices makes this case a common one. Identify the parts, replace each with its equivalent, and repeat until a single resistance remains. The process is more time consuming than difficult, and it lets you apply Ohm's law to a circuit that is not one loop.

concepts.name: IR drop in wires
concepts.statement: Wire resistance sits in series with the devices it feeds, so the current the devices draw produces an $IR$ drop in the wires and the voltage left for the devices is less than the source's. When a device of very low resistance switches on, the large current it draws makes that drop large, and everything else on the same wires receives less voltage. It is why the refrigerator light dims when the motor comes on and why a worn or very long extension cord wastes power.

concepts.name: Resistor
concepts.statement: A resistor is a component made to have a definite resistance, and in a circuit diagram every device that converts electrical energy, from a lamp to a heater, is drawn as one.

concepts.name: Electromotive force
concepts.statement: Every voltage source, whether it is a battery, a generator, a solar cell or a thermoelectric device, creates a potential difference that can drive current through a resistance. That potential difference, measured when no current flows, is called the electromotive force, or emf. Emf is not a force at all; it is a special type of potential difference, and its unit is the volt. It is set by the source's construction, such as the particular combination of chemicals in a battery.

concepts.name: Internal resistance
concepts.statement: Every voltage source has two fundamental parts, a source of electrical energy and an internal resistance, and the two are in series. The internal resistance is the inherent resistance to the flow of current within the source itself, and the smaller it is for a given emf, the more current and the more power the source can supply. It is why a truck battery and a motorcycle battery of the same emf are not interchangeable, and it rises as a battery is depleted.

concepts.name: Terminal voltage
concepts.statement: The voltage measured across a source's terminals is its emf less the voltage drop across its own internal resistance, so the larger the current drawn, or the larger the internal resistance, the smaller the terminal voltage. Terminal voltage equals emf only when no current flows. This one equation explains why car lights dim gradually as a battery runs down instead of blinking off, and why a battery tester measures the voltage under a load.

concepts.name: Current delivered to a load
concepts.statement: The internal resistance is in series with the load, so the total resistance of the circuit is the load plus the internal resistance and Ohm's law gives the current. The smaller the internal resistance, the greater the current a source supplies to a given load. When a battery ages and its internal resistance becomes a significant fraction of the load, the current falls noticeably, which is what a worn battery in a flashlight or a starter motor shows.

concepts.name: Sources in series
concepts.statement: When voltage sources are connected in series, their emfs add algebraically and their internal resistances add, so a row of cells produces a larger total emf than one cell. Cells put into an appliance backward subtract instead of adding. The disadvantage of the series connection is that the internal resistances add too, which is what limited the author's two six-volt batteries in place of one twelve-volt battery.

concepts.name: Sources in parallel
concepts.statement: Two identical sources connected in parallel produce the same total emf as one of them, since each has the same potential difference, but their internal resistances are in parallel and so the total internal resistance is smaller than either. The parallel connection therefore delivers more current to a load than one source could. Some diesel cars use two twelve-volt batteries in parallel for exactly this reason: twelve volts, and enough current to turn a diesel engine.

concepts.name: Charging a battery
concepts.statement: You recharge a battery by passing current through it opposite to the current it supplies, which reverses its chemical reaction. The charger's emf must therefore be larger than the battery's. The two sources are then in series with their emfs opposed, so the difference of the emfs and the sum of the internal resistances set the current. While a battery charges, its terminal voltage is greater than its emf, since the current in $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ is now negative.

concepts.name: Battery emf from chemistry
concepts.statement: A chemical reaction in the cell separates charge, driving electrons onto the anode and removing them from the cathode, and the energy the reaction gives each electron is what fixes the voltage. In a lead-acid cell the reaction gives each electron about two electron volts, and since an electron volt is the energy a single electron gains through one volt, the cell produces about two volts. A different reaction gives a different energy and so a different voltage, and because the reacting substances have resistance, no emf can be made without an internal resistance.

concepts.name: Kirchhoff’s rules from conservation laws
concepts.statement: Many circuits do not reduce to combinations of series and parallel parts, and for those you need two rules that hold for any circuit at all. Both are conservation laws in circuit form: the junction rule applies conservation of charge to a point where wires meet, and the loop rule applies conservation of energy to a closed path. Because they are conservation laws, they apply to simple circuits as well, and the series and parallel rules follow from them.

concepts.name: Junction rule
concepts.statement: Current is the flow of charge and charge is conserved, so whatever charge flows into a junction in a given time must flow out of it in the same time; charge cannot pile up at a point in a wire. The sum of the currents entering a junction therefore equals the sum of the currents leaving it. Each junction gives one equation, and together with the loop rule these equations are what determine the unknown currents in a network.

concepts.name: Loop rule
concepts.statement: Around any closed path the algebraic sum of the changes in potential must be zero, because a charge carried around the loop returns to where it started and must have the same potential energy there. Whatever energy the emf supplies is transferred into other forms by the devices in the loop, so the emf equals the sum of the $IR$ drops. Each independent loop gives one more equation, and as many independent equations as unknowns are needed to solve the circuit.

concepts.name: Signs in the loop rule
concepts.statement: Applying the rules means making two choices, a direction for each unknown current and a direction around each loop, and neither choice can be wrong: a current assumed backwards simply comes out negative, and a loop traversed the other way reverses every sign in its equation. What must be consistent are the four sign cases. A resistor traversed with the current changes the potential by $-IR$ and against the current by $+IR$; an emf traversed from minus to plus contributes $+\mathcal{E}$ and from plus to minus $-\mathcal{E}$.

concepts.name: Applying Kirchhoff’s rules
concepts.statement: Apply the junction rule at junctions until each new equation brings in a current the earlier ones did not. Apply the loop rule to as many loops as you need to match the number of unknowns. Then solve the simultaneous equations and check the answers for sign and size. A negative current means only that the assumed direction was the opposite one. Checking that the currents still satisfy the junction rule catches most algebraic mistakes.

concepts.name: Kirchhoff’s rules
concepts.statement: Kirchhoff's rules are the junction rule and the loop rule together, two statements of conservation that let you analyze any circuit, simple or complex.

concepts.name: Conservation laws
concepts.statement: The conservation laws require that energy and charge be conserved in a system, and in a circuit they become Kirchhoff's two rules.

concepts.name: Voltmeter in parallel
concepts.statement: A voltmeter measures the potential difference across a device, and objects in parallel have the same potential difference, so place the meter in parallel with whatever you want to measure. Measure a terminal voltage the same way, across the terminals of the source. That is also why the meter can never reach the emf itself: the internal resistance is always included.

concepts.name: Ammeter in series
concepts.statement: An ammeter measures the current in a branch, and objects in series carry the same current, so the meter is placed in series in the branch to be measured and all of that current passes through it. Anywhere in the same series branch gives the same reading. Connecting an ammeter in parallel with a resistor instead can damage it, since the meter's low resistance would then take most of the circuit's current.

concepts.name: Galvanometer
concepts.statement: The heart of most analog meters is a galvanometer, a device whose needle deflects in proportion to the current through it. Two numbers describe one: its resistance and its current sensitivity, the current that gives a full-scale deflection. A galvanometer of $50\ \mu\text{A}$ sensitivity reads half scale at $25\ \mu\text{A}$, and with a $25\text{-}\Omega$ resistance it needs only 1.25 mV across it to read full scale. Everything a voltmeter or an ammeter can do is this one device with one resistor added.

concepts.name: Galvanometer as voltmeter
concepts.statement: To read a given voltage at full scale, the total resistance of the meter must be that voltage divided by the galvanometer's current sensitivity. The galvanometer's own resistance is tiny by comparison, so nearly all of that resistance is the one in series with it. The larger the voltage to measure, the larger that resistance must be, and switching different resistances into series gives a meter its several scales.

concepts.name: Galvanometer as ammeter
concepts.statement: A small resistance in parallel with the galvanometer sends nearly all of the current around it. The instrument can then read currents far larger than the one that deflects its needle fully, and the galvanometer stays protected. Since the shunt and the galvanometer have the same voltage across them, the shunt's resistance is the galvanometer's resistance scaled by the ratio of the galvanometer's current to the total. The larger the current to measure, the smaller the shunt must be.

concepts.name: Meters altering a circuit
concepts.statement: A voltmeter is another resistance in parallel and an ammeter another resistance in series, so every measurement changes the circuit it measures. The effect is negligible only when the voltmeter's resistance is far larger than that of the device it sits across, and the ammeter's is far smaller than that of the branch it sits in. A voltmeter of comparable resistance halves the parallel resistance, and an ammeter of comparable resistance halves the current. The inaccuracy is not a fault in the meter, and nothing removes it entirely.

concepts.name: Voltmeter
concepts.statement: A voltmeter is an instrument that measures the potential difference between two points, the voltage across whatever it is connected to.

concepts.name: Ammeter
concepts.statement: An ammeter is an instrument that measures the current through the branch of a circuit in which it is placed.

concepts.name: Analog meter
concepts.statement: An analog meter gives its reading as the position of a needle over a marked scale, and most are built around a galvanometer.

concepts.name: Digital meter
concepts.statement: A digital meter gives its reading as a number on a display, measuring the quantity with electronic circuits rather than a moving needle.

concepts.name: Full-scale deflection
concepts.statement: The full-scale deflection of a meter is the largest reading its needle can show, and the current that gives it is the galvanometer's current sensitivity.

concepts.name: Shunt resistance
concepts.statement: A shunt resistance is a small resistance connected in parallel with a galvanometer, so that most of the current passes around the galvanometer and the combination can measure larger currents.

concepts.name: Current sensitivity
concepts.statement: The current sensitivity of a galvanometer is the current that gives it a full-scale deflection.

concepts.name: Null measurement
concepts.statement: Standard meters alter the circuit they measure because they must draw some current to work. A null measurement instead balances the circuit until no current at all flows through the measuring device, so it disturbs nothing and senses the quantity directly. Null methods are more accurate but more complex than standard meters, and they still have limits: the balance is never exactly zero, and the standards they rely on carry their own uncertainties.

concepts.name: Potentiometer
concepts.statement: A steady current down a long uniform wire makes the potential fall evenly along it, so a contact at the right place picks off any voltage between zero and the full drop. Connect an unknown emf in opposition through a galvanometer and move the contact until the needle reads zero. No current then flows through the unknown, so the balance point measures the emf itself rather than a terminal voltage. Repeating the balance with a known standard emf makes the unknown emf a ratio of two wire lengths, with the current canceling out.

concepts.name: Ohmmeter
concepts.statement: The common ohmmeters apply a voltage to a resistance, measure the current and report the quotient as the resistance. Their accuracy is limited, because the two meters they use alter both the voltage across the resistor and the current through it. Measuring the terminal voltage rather than assuming the source's is better. But the voltage is most accurate when the current is small, and the current is most accurate when it is large, so the two cannot both be at their best.

concepts.name: Wheatstone bridge
concepts.statement: A Wheatstone bridge arranges two known resistances and one variable one in two branches, with a galvanometer bridging them. Adjust the variable arm until the galvanometer reads zero. The two bridged points are then at the same potential and no current crosses the bridge, so the galvanometer disturbs nothing. Equating the $IR$ drops along the matching parts of the two branches and taking their ratio leaves the unknown resistance as a product and a quotient of the three known ones, with the currents canceled out.

concepts.name: Bridge device
concepts.statement: A bridge device connects two branches of a circuit through a meter, and adjusting it until the meter reads zero lets one quantity be found by a null measurement.

concepts.name: RC circuit
concepts.statement: A circuit containing a resistor and a capacitor behaves differently from a purely resistive one, because the capacitor's voltage $V_{\text{c}} = Q/C$ grows as charge collects on its plates and opposes the source. The current begins at $I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R$, when all of the potential difference is across the resistor, and falls to zero as the capacitor's voltage rises to the emf. The smaller the resistance, the faster a given capacitor charges, and the resistance includes the source's internal resistance and the wires.

concepts.name: Charging a capacitor
concepts.statement: The voltage across a charging capacitor rises steeply at first, when the current is largest, and then more and more slowly as the capacitor's own voltage opposes the source. The approach to the emf is exponential and asymptotic: the final value is never quite reached, though after a few multiples of the time constant the difference no longer matters. The same equation is what fixes how long a flash unit, a timing circuit or a pacemaker must wait between pulses.

concepts.name: Time constant
concepts.statement: The product of the resistance and the capacitance has units of seconds and sets the pace of the whole circuit. A small resistance lets a larger current flow, and a small capacitance needs less charge, so either makes the circuit faster; both facts are contained in $\tau = RC$. Because the exponent in both exponential laws is $-t/RC$, the time constant is the only time in the problem, and every statement about charging and discharging is a statement about multiples of it.

concepts.name: Discharging a capacitor
concepts.statement: A charged capacitor discharged through a resistor drives its own current, largest at the start when its voltage is highest, and its voltage falls exponentially with the same time constant. A flash discharges far faster than it charges because the ionized gas of the flash tube has a much smaller resistance than the battery that charged it, and it is that brevity, less than a microsecond, that freezes a hummingbird's wings or a bullet in flight.

concepts.name: Fraction per time constant
concepts.statement: Setting $t = \tau$ in the charging law gives $V = \mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-1}) = 0.632\mathcal{E}$, so in every time constant the voltage covers 0.632 of the distance that remains. In the discharging law it gives $V = 0.368V_0$, so the voltage falls to 0.368 of its value in every time constant. That is the character of an exponential: the fraction, not the amount, is the same in each interval, so the voltage approaches its final value but never reaches it.

concepts.name: RC timing circuits
concepts.statement: Because the time constant is set by a resistance and a capacitance the designer chooses, an RC circuit is a clock. A lamp whose resistance collapses at a threshold voltage charges, flashes, discharges and starts again, at a rate the resistance sets; the same arrangement sets the interval of an intermittent windshield wiper and the rhythm an artificial pacemaker supplies to a heart. Adjusting the resistance adjusts the time between pulses.
